# Expedites, tier-2 risk and calibration - generated by `extend.py`, not hand-edited

## 1. Expedites

Premium = real unit cost x (premium multiple - 1) x the part's shortfall quantity. The multiples (air 4x, partial 1.8x, overtime 1.25x) and the lead-time compression are assumptions.

| part | vendor | mode | lead mean | days saved | shortfall units | premium | needed? |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Part_0038 | V09 | air freight | 6.8 d | 3.7 d | 76,654 | $229,962 | no |
| Part_0038 | V09 | partial shipment | 6.8 d | 2.0 d | 76,654 | $61,323 | no |
| Part_0038 | V09 | supplier overtime | 6.8 d | 1.0 d | 76,654 | $19,164 | no |
| Part_0172 | V16 | air freight | 10.4 d | 5.7 d | 4,618 | $2,355 | no |
| Part_0172 | V16 | partial shipment | 10.4 d | 3.1 d | 4,618 | $628 | no |
| Part_0172 | V16 | supplier overtime | 10.4 d | 1.6 d | 4,618 | $196 | no |
| Part_0027 | V01 | air freight | 4.0 d | 2.2 d | 921 | $1,547 | no |
| Part_0027 | V01 | partial shipment | 4.0 d | 1.2 d | 921 | $413 | no |
| Part_0027 | V01 | supplier overtime | 4.0 d | 0.6 d | 921 | $129 | no |
| Part_0152 | V07 | air freight | 6.1 d | 3.4 d | 71,157 | $53,368 | no |
| Part_0152 | V07 | partial shipment | 6.1 d | 1.8 d | 71,157 | $14,231 | no |
| Part_0152 | V07 | supplier overtime | 6.1 d | 0.9 d | 71,157 | $4,447 | no |

**0 of 24 options are needed.** Every top driver still has time to be ordered at its normal lead time, because the real part lead times are short (median 9 days). Paying for speed would not help: these parts are short on quantity, not on time. In the simulated version (lead times of 14-75 days) 11 of 24 expedites arrived too late; with real lead times the question does not come up.

## 2. Tier 2: the factories behind the vendors (real)

SCMS records a manufacturing site on every line. Across the 27 vendors there are **59 sites**; **27 of them ship through more than one vendor**, and 7 vendors rely on a single site.

**GSK Mississauga (Canada)** sits behind 4 vendors a buyer would see as separate, 32 parts and 17 of the 17 products. The vendor-to-site link is real; the site-to-part link goes through the assumed vendor mapping, so the part and product counts show the method, not a fact about power tools.

## 3. Calibration against simulated futures

Draw 60 independent futures from the same model, treat each as what happened, and ask how often the fan (from 150 simulations) contained it.

| product | % inside P10-P90 | % below P10 | % above P90 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Manuf_0032 | 100% | 0% | 0% |
| Manuf_0033 | 99% | 0% | 1% |
| Manuf_0034 | 98% | 0% | 2% |
| Manuf_0035 | 99% | 0% | 1% |
| Manuf_0036 | 99% | 0% | 1% |
| Manuf_0037 | 99% | 0% | 1% |
| Manuf_0038 | 97% | 1% | 2% |
| Manuf_0039 | 100% | 0% | 0% |
| Manuf_0040 | 96% | 1% | 3% |
| Manuf_0041 | 99% | 1% | 1% |
| Manuf_0042 | 98% | 1% | 1% |
| Manuf_0043 | 100% | 0% | 0% |
| Manuf_0044 | 99% | 0% | 1% |
| Manuf_0045 | 99% | 0% | 1% |
| Manuf_0046 | 99% | 1% | 1% |
| Manuf_0047 | 98% | 1% | 1% |
| Manuf_0048 | 98% | 1% | 1% |

**Mean coverage 99% against a target of 80%.** 
The band is too wide for its label, and here it is also very narrow in units: the real part lead-time distributions have little spread (two to four values a few days apart), and buildable units are whole numbers, so many weeks have P10 = P50 = P90 and almost every future lands on it. The fan's width comes from supply timing, and in this chain timing barely moves the answer; quantity does.

The futures come from the same model as the fan, so this checks the propagation, not whether real lead times behave this way.
